# Urban renewable energy and ecosystems: integrating vegetation with ground-mounted solar arrays increases arthropod abundance of key functional groups

& & John H. Armstrong[1,2] Andy J. Kulikowski II[1] Stacy M. Philpott[1]

> Accepted: 29 September 2020 / Published online: 12 October 2020 # Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2020

## Abstract

Cities are increasingly developing renewable energy within urban areas, yet the implications for ecosystems have not been explored. This study brings together climate change mitigation policies and ecosystem conservation in urban areas by investigating how ground-mounted solar arrays in parking lots affect arthropod abundance and biodiversity. We assess which arthropods are present under these solar canopies and investigate how integration of vegetation under the solar arrays affects arthropod abundance, abundance of different functional groups, and family richness. We sampled arthropods, collected data on habitat characteristics, and evaluated landscape cover within 2 km of eight study sites around San Jose and Santa Cruz, California. We found substantial abundance and diversity of arthropods underneath ground-mounted solar arrays in urban area parking lots, and that arrays integrated with vegetation have significantly greater arthropod abundance and more detritivores, parasitoids, and family richness. The results demonstrate that ground-mounted solar arrays in parking lots, especially when integrated with vegetation, can be a win-win for climate mitigation, arthropod richness, and ecosystem functioning.

Keywords Urban solar energy[. ] Arthropods[. ] Urban ecology[. ] Reconciliation ecology[. ] Urban biodiversity

## Introduction

Urban areas simultaneously face direct impacts and the challenges of addressing climate change and biodiversity loss. In response to the climate crisis, a growing number of cities are enacting greenhouse gas (GHG) emission mitigation policies and are looking to develop renewable energy within their jurisdictional boundaries (Armstrong 2019; Rosenzweig et al. 2010; Yi 2013). In addition to rooftop solar panels, groundmounted solar arrays are increasingly being built in urban parking lots, fields, parks, and other spaces (Gagnon et al. 2016). Many cities are in biodiversity-rich areas such as

floodplains, estuaries, and coastlines. By 2030, urban land cover in biodiversity hotspots is expected to increase significantly and is projected to affect more than 25% of all endangered or critically endangered species (CBD 2012; Elmqvist et al. 2013; Wilkinson et al. 2013). Given the importance of urban ecosystems and urban biodiversity, it is critical that ecologists and planners consider the ecosystem effects of urban renewable energy development and undertake proper planning to ensure the best possible outcomes.

This study brings together climate change mitigation strategies and biodiversity conservation in urban areas by investigating how ground-mounted solar arrays in parking lots affect arthropod biodiversity. With mounting solar energy development, these ‘solar parking canopies’ (also known as solar carports), under which cars park, are increasingly common. Parking lots comprise up to 20% of the surface area of typical cities (Akbari and Rosa 2008; Gilbert et al. 2017) and have a great deal of potential for future solar development (Gagnon et al. 2016). At the same time, as impervious surfaces span large areas throughout urban spaces, parking lots are associated with negative environmental and ecosystem impacts, including habitat fragmentation, water runoff, pollution, and heat island effects (Davis et al. 2010).

Interest in urban solar energy has come from city governments seeking to deploy renewable energy locally and amidst concerns about the impacts of rural utility-scale solar energy, including harm to ecosystems and species like the desert tortoise (Hernandez et al. 2014, 2016). Hernandez et al. (2015) found that solar energy in the built environment in California – in urban and semi-urban areas – could exceed the state’s energy needs, with open and green space comprising a third of the compatible areas. As of November 2019, California already had 17,365 completed ground-mounted solar installations and applications for 17,634 more, demonstrating that there is significant prior and planned development.[1]

From a reconciliation ecology perspective, which seeks to create urban-natural habitats where flora and fauna are incorporated into the built environment (Handel et al. 2013; Rosenzweig 2003), solar parking canopies introduce a structure into impervious parking lot surfaces. Green spaces such as garden areas are sometimes incorporated with solar parking canopies, which may offer habitat areas and the potential to “green” parking lots (U.S. EPA 2008) if integrated with vegetation such as flowers, grasses, and shrubs. Green spaces can help reduce negative environmental effects of urban development and high concentrations of impervious services (Solecki et al. 2005; Spronken-Smith and Oke 1998). In various forms, green spaces contribute to environmental sustainability, ecosystem services, and provide aesthetic appeal (Breuste et al. 2013; Haq 2011). Reconciliation ecology and other ecosystem- and biodiversity-minded approaches are important to consider in a variety of applications as the pace and scale of urbanization increases.

Solar parking canopies, especially if integrated with vegetation, may serve as habitat area for arthropods, which are affected by urbanization as a result of habitat changes, fragmentation, invasive species, and other anthropogenic pressures (Christie et al. 2010; McIntyre 2000). Arthropods serve critical roles in urban ecosystems as fundamental components of trophic networks and in providing essential ecosystem services (Bolger et al. 2000; McIntyre 2000; Sanford et al. 2009). Accordingly, various arthropod functional groups (e.g., predators and pollinators) – and richness generally – are important for a range of services such as pest control and nutrient cycling (Buchori and Sahari 2008; Nsengimana et al. 2018; Sattler et al. 2010).

While characteristics vary, small and informal urban habitat areas and green spaces can support substantial arthropod abundance including diverse arthropod communities (Bolger et al. 2000; Gibb and Hochuli 2002; Noordijk et al. 2010; Rupprecht et al. 2015). Landscape and local factors can also

The data are publicly available at californiadgstats.ca.gov (last accessed February 12, 2020). We were not able to distinguish between urban and rural settings or the percentage in parking lots.

be important in driving arthropod abundance and diversity in these urban habitat areas (Magura et al. 2010; Philpott et al. 2014; Rudd et al. 2002). Landscape factors known to affect arthropod communities include habitat connectivity, habitat fragment size, the extent of development, and distance to natural areas (Egerer et al. 2017; Faeth et al. 2012; Magura et al. 2010; Philpott et al. 2014; Rudd et al. 2002; Yamaguchi 2004). Important local habitat characteristics include vegetation traits such as height and floral availability (Bennett and Gratton 2013; Lerman et al. 2018; McKinney 2008; Uno et al. 2010). These landscape and local characteristics can also affect arthropod richness, which is important for biodiversity and ecosystem services in urban areas (Egerer et al. 2017; Philpott et al. 2014).

Here, we address how solar parking canopy presence may affect arthropod communities in urban areas. Because arthropod response to solar canopies remains unexplored, we assess which groups of arthropods are using such canopies and in what abundance. We determine how integration of vegetation and landscape context may affect overall arthropod abundance, abundance of different functional groups, and arthropod richness. Specifically, we ask, (1) What arthropod groups are found under urban solar parking canopies and in what abundance? (2) How does integration of vegetation with urban solar parking canopies affect arthropod abundance and abundance of key functional groups? (3) Does landscape context influence how integration of vegetation under solar parking canopies affects arthropods? And (4) are there differences in arthropod family richness between solar parking canopies with and without vegetation? We hypothesized that there would be greater arthropod abundance and richness under solar parking canopies integrated with vegetation and that there would be an interaction effect between landscape factors associated with biodiversity, such as forest cover, and vegetation under solar canopies. Thus, we assessed what arthropod groups are present and the potential for this kind of renewable energy development to provide urban ecosystem conservation opportunities. This general assessment serves to evaluate the overall habitat potential under these structures to inform ecosystem and biodiversity planning.

## Methodology

## Study sites

We identified eight study sites (Fig. 1) in urban areas that met three criteria: 1) presence of both a vegetated solar parking canopy (vegetation at least 3 m × 3 m under or immediately adjacent to the solar canopy) and an isolated solar parking canopy (no vegetation under the solar canopy and at least 15 m from the nearest vegetation); 2) solar parking canopies and vegetation areas that had been present for at least three

Fig. 1 Map of study sites in the San Jose and Santa Cruz, California areas (buffers from the vegetated solar canopies). The landscape characteristics are from the 2016 National Land Cover Database. The solar parking canopies in the sites closest together are 2.03 km apart

years; and 3) each site must be at least 2 km from the nearest site. The presence or absence of vegetation under/adjacent to the solar canopies comprise our two paired treatments (‘vegetated’ and ‘isolated’ solar canopies). To find sites that met these criteria, we used Google Satellite and Street View to review major schools and colleges around the cities of San Jose and Santa Cruz, California, and then went in person to evaluate whether they met the criteria. We looked at schools because many of them in the region installed such solar canopies in the last ten years and because we could assume that human activities at schools are relatively similar. We selected seven sites in and around San Jose (37.3382° N, 121.8863° W) and its suburbs (within Santa Clara County), and one site in Santa Cruz (36.9741° N, 122.0308° W). The site in Santa Cruz is Harbor High School and the seven sites around San Jose are Andrew P. Hill High School, Foothills College, Freemont High School, Homestead High School, Lynbrook High School, Santa Theresa High School, and William C. Overfelt High School. The mean distance between the vegetated and isolated solar canopies at each site is 203 m (SE ± 74), measured from the center of each solar canopy.

## Landscape and habitat characteristics

We assessed landscape characteristics surrounding each solar canopy with geographic information system (GIS), using 2016 data from the National Land Cover Database (see Fig. 1) (Jin

et al. 2013; Wickham et al. 2014). We created four major landuse categories: a) agriculture, combining pasture/hay [NLCD number 81] and cultivated crops, [82]; b) developed land, combining low, medium, and high intensity [22, 23, 24]; c) developed open space (which includes grass and planted vegetation) [21]; and d) natural land use, combining deciduous forest [41], evergreen forest [42] mixed forest [43], shrub/scrub [52], and herbaceous [71] and woody wetlands [90]. We used spatial analysis tools in ArcMap (v 10.7.1) to calculate the percentage of each land cover type within 100 m, 1 km, and 2 km, buffers surrounding each vegetated and isolated solar canopy. While the sites are all surrounded by substantial development, limiting differences among these land-use categories between sites, there is still variation (see electronic supplementary material Table S1).

In addition to these factors, we quantified a variety of local characteristics at all sites (Table 1). We measured the distance from the center of the solar parking canopies to the nearest other vegetation (e.g., a row of trees or a field). We measured temperature under each solar canopy using temperature loggers (Onset HOBO UA-001-08), placed approximately 20 cm under the center end of each solar canopy and set to record temperature data (°C) every hour for the entire time of all sampling. We measured solar canopy incline using an inclinometer. Under the eight vegetated solar canopies, we also measured the vegetation area, floral availability, and shortest and tallest vegetation present during each sampling period.

The primary type of vegetation varied across the eight vegetated solar canopies. Three sites were primarily comprised of bushes, three of grasses and weeds, and two of grasses and ornamental flowers. The three sites with bushes also had some grasses and weeds. The variation in the vegetation is a limitation of this study, but it also reflects common real-world differences.

## Sticky trap sampling and arthropod identification

Given that arthropod emergence and activity vary across seasons, we sampled at three different times during 2018: April, June, and August.[2] At each site and during each sampling period, we used yellow sticky traps (15.24 cm × 20.32 cm) to collect arthropods to identify and measure abundance. We placed six traps under each vegetated and isolated solar canopy during each sampling period for a total of 18 traps per canopy over the three sampling periods. Sticky trap placement was standardized for consistency across sites, with four sticky traps hung 30 cm beneath the top of each solar canopy on each side of the two major support stanchions (posts) and two sticky traps hung approximately 75 cm above the ground by each of the stanchions. Based on the construction of the stanchions, which have wider round cement supports at that height, the lower sticky traps were still separate from the vegetation even where it was tall. Sticky traps were left out for seven days each time. When collected, we covered sticky traps with wax paper and stored them in a refrigerator and later identified arthropods. As expected, some sticky traps were lost at each site due to wind, birds, or human activity, but 199 of 276 were successfully collected.

2 At one site, Harbor High School, we were only able to sample in April and June.

We identified arthropods on one side of each sticky trap (standardized based on whether the side pointed to the middle of the canopy) to order and family when possible, following Borror and White (1970) and Marshall (2006). We classified arthropods to six functional groups (detritivores, herbivores, parasitoids, pollinators, predators, and sanguivores) based on Borror and White (1970), Marshall (2006), and additional literature sources (Bellamy et al. 2018; Kenneth et al. 1991). We assessed functional groups to consider how ecosystem roles might be affected by canopy type or placement within the landscape.

As with other studies that utilize sticky traps for arthropod collection, some functional groups may be under-represented by this sampling methodology (Yi et al. 2012). For instance, spiders may avoid them. Pollinator counts may be lower than if arthropods were collected using standardized bowl traps. Ground-dwelling arthropods may be under-represented compared to studies that utilize pitfall traps. Sticky traps were the best sampling method for this study, however, given their flexibility and the ability to hang them under the solar canopies.

## Data analysis

To determine what arthropod groups were under solar parking canopies and in what abundance, we present descriptive results for the number of arthropods collected and common orders and functional groups. This provides a general assessment of the habitat potential of solar parking canopies and which arthropods utilize them.

We used generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) to compare overall arthropod abundance and abundance within functional groups (response variables) between vegetated and isolated solar canopies. Because models with Poisson distributed errors were overdispersed, we used negative binomial

errors distributions for all analyses. We included a random blocking effect to account for unexplained variance between sites and sampling periods (nested within sites). We also examined the influence of landscape variables (distance to other vegetation, temperature, solar canopy incline, and percentage of the surrounding landscape in agriculture, developed land, developed open space, and natural land use at 100 m, 1 km, and 2 km buffers) on each response variable by constructing models that included solar array treatment (vegetated or isolated), each landscape variable separately, and the interaction between the two. We assessed model fit using Akaike Information Criterion (AICc) and, for each response, chose the models that had the lowest AICc score.

Among the vegetated canopies, we used the same GLMMs to examine the influence of vegetation characteristics (floral abundance, vegetation area, minimum vegetation height, and maximum vegetation eight) on arthropod abundance and arthropod functional groups (response variables), and to assess the interaction between vegetation characteristics and landscape variables.

To investigate differences in arthropod richness depending on solar canopy treatment, we calculated family accumulation curves by treatment using the ‘vegan’ package in R (Oksanen 2013), as well as non-parametric richness estimator Chao1 values (Chao and Chiu 2001). We used generalized linear models (GLMs) to compare Chao1 values for estimated arthropod family richness (response variable) between vegetated and isolated solar canopies at the site level using a gamma distribution.

To visualize potential differences in community composition of arthropod families between solar canopy treatments, we used non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) fit with Bray-Curtis dissimilarity in three dimensions. We also conducted a permutational analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) on the centroid and variances of both solar canopy treatments to test for differences in arthropod family community composition. Community analyses were conducted in R v.3.6.3 (R Core Team 2019) using the vegan package (Oksanen 2013).

## Results

## Arthropod abundance

We collected a total of 3318 arthropods from the 199 sticky traps recovered. We identified 3294 of the arthropods to order and 2137 to family, representing a total of 12 orders (10 under vegetated solar canopies, 10 under isolated solar canopies) and 63 families (54 under vegetated solar canopies, 40 under isolated solar canopies). Common orders (more than 60 individuals collected) included Hemiptera (1080 individuals, 32.55% of arthropods collected), Diptera (961, 28.96%),

Hymenoptera (565, 17.03%), Thysanoptera (488, 14.71%), Araneae (65, 1.96%), and Coleoptera (60, 1.81%).

We found that vegetated solar canopies had significantly greater arthropod abundance than isolated solar canopies (F1,196 = 7.456, p = 0.007) (Fig. 2). Overall, vegetated solar canopies (sticky trap n = 101) accounted for 1989 arthropods compared to 1285 from isolated solar canopies (sticky trap n = 98), or 43% more under vegetated solar canopies (40.1% accounting for the difference in the number of sticky traps).

No landscape variables nor their interactions with solar canopy treatment improved model fit except for developed open space at 100 m, which significantly increased total arthropod abundance (F1,196 = 6.769, p = 0.010). Among the vegetated solar canopies, floral availability had a significant positive effect on arthropod abundance (F1,99 = 4.491, p = 0.037) and a significant positive effect on herbivore abundance (F1,99 = 13.972, p = <0.0001). None of the other vegetation characteristics or interactions between them and landscape characteristics had a significant effect on arthropod abundance or abundance of any other functional groups.

## Arthropod functional group abundance

There were significantly more detritivores (F1,197 = 13.799 p < 0.0001) and parasitoids (F1,197 = 7.468, p = 0.007) under vegetated solar canopies than under isolated solar canopies (Fig. 3). Abundance of other functional groups did not differ with canopy type (Table 2). While there were more herbivores at vegetated solar canopies than isolated solar canopies (1010 versus 668), there was substantial variation and there was not a statistically distinguishable difference by treatment, despite a significant positive effect of floral abundance among just the vegetated canopies.

## Arthropod family richness

Family accumulation curves among all vegetated and isolated solar canopies appear to be reaching their asymptotes (Fig. 4), indicating that sampling was exhaustive enough to make comparisons. The combined isolated solar canopy curve crosses under the vegetated solar canopy curve, which is increasing but flattening out. Based on Chao1 estimates, family richness was significantly greater (p = 0.001) among vegetated solar canopies (63.231 ± SE 6.164) than among isolated solar canopies (42.625 ± 2.826) (total number of families by site and treatment are listed in electronic supplementary material Table S2).

The NMDS plot (stress = 0.11) comparing community composition of arthropod families suggests that vegetated solar canopies have similar composition to one another whereas isolated solar canopies exhibit a higher degree of dissimilarly (electronic supplementary material Fig. S1). ## Discussion

We found that arthropod abundance was significantly greater under urban solar parking canopies that are integrated with vegetation than those isolated from vegetation. Vegetated solar canopies had over 40% more arthropods than isolated solar canopies. There was a variety of arthropods under solar parking canopies, including 12 orders and 63 families, with significantly greater arthropod family richness under vegetated solar canopies. Such arthropod diversity is important in supporting broader ecosystem biodiversity and functioning

(Lagucki et al. 2017; McIntyre 2000). As urban biodiversity planning proceeds, including restoration ecology in urban areas, arthropod richness is a critical consideration (Handel et al. 2013).

Both the visual inspection of the NMDS plot and marginally significant result of the PERMANOVA suggest some distinction in community composition of arthropod families between solar canopy treatments. The higher degree of similarity between vegetated canopies may indicate that local vegetation is a strong driver of arthropod community composition. Some isolated canopies had high community similarity to vegetated canopies, but many sites were quite distinct, suggesting that other factors such as variation on the landscape could be driving community composition in the absence of vegetation.

Vegetated solar canopies had significantly greater abundance of parasitoids and detritivores, both of which are beneficial arthropod groups for urban ecosystem functioning and services (Free et al. 1975; Hogg et al. 2011; Jones and Leather

2012; Matteson and Langellotto 2011). Parasitoids are especially important for ecosystems given that they function at high trophic levels and promote diversity and stability in insect communities (Fenoglio and Salvo 2010; Shaw and Hochberg 2001). They are essential in maintaining ecosystem functions and regulating insect pest populations (Buchori and Sahari 2008). The presence of parasitoids translates to having more organisms being parasitized, indicating greater ecosystem integrity (Buchori and Sahari 2008).

It makes sense that vegetated solar canopies have more detritivores considering the presence of organic matter to decompose, which also points to the benefit of those green spaces. Detritivores serve foundational ecosystem functioning roles in bottom-up interactions and nutrient cycling (Seastedt and Crossley 1984). Their abundance and diversity are instrumental in maintaining soil quality and organic material turnover (Nsengimana et al. 2018; Paoletti et al. 2007). In their consumption and transformation of detritus, detritivores have

Fig. 4 Arthropod family accumulation curves for all vegetated and isolated solar parking canopies

a substantial effect on food webs and have consequences for community structures (Yang 2006).

Of the landscape characteristics, only developed open space at close proximity (100 m) had a significant effect on total arthropod abundance. The positive effect of developed open space is likely because that land-cover category includes grass and planted vegetation, which can support greater abundance of arthropods (Philpott et al. 2014). Neither developed open space nor other landscape characteristics had a significant effect on individual arthropod functional groups. The effect on total abundance but not any functional groups may be due to sample size limitations and variation. The strong influence of vegetation integration on arthropod abundance, and not of landscape characteristics other than open space at 100 m, is surprising given that in other urban systems, landscape factors strongly drive arthropod abundance (Magura et al. 2010; Philpott et al. 2014; Rudd et al. 2002). This could partially be because the solar canopy sites are largely developed and the differences in the surrounding land use cover may not be as significant as in other cases.

Among the vegetated solar canopies and vegetation characteristics, floral availability had a significant positive effect on arthropod abundance overall and on herbivore abundance. The role of floral abundance is likely because some arthropod functional groups rely on flowers. In other vegetated urban habitats, such as community gardens and lawns, flowers support pollinators, parasitoids, and arthropod richness generally (Bennett and Gratton 2012, 2013; Lerman et al. 2018; Matteson and Langellotto 2011), although effects vary among some arthropods (Burks and Philpott 2017). Although floral abundance had a significant positive effect on herbivore abundance among vegetated canopies, there was no difference in herbivore abundance between vegetated and isolated arrays. This is likely due to relatively large variation in herbivore numbers in different sites.

To the authors’ knowledge and based on a comprehensive review of renewable energy and biodiversity by Gasparatos

et al. (2017), no prior studies have examined arthropod, ecosystem, or biodiversity implications of urban ground-mounted solar energy. This is the first study to examine how vegetation and landscape context influence arthropods under urban solar canopies. The most relevant research comes from a study in London, where Nash et al. (2015) found that integration of rooftop solar arrays with green roofs enhances biodiversity by providing a microhabitat for insects and birds, and by providing shade that increases diversity in vegetation patches. While green roofs and the solar panels placed on them are different, these findings generally align with ours. So do findings from a study in a rural desert setting in Chile, where Suuronen et al. (2017) found that ground-mounted solar arrays created shady conditions and microclimate changes that provided habitat for arthropods.

Our findings also align with research showing that relatively small urban green spaces and habitat areas can be important for conserving arthropods and supporting biodiversity, and that these areas can provide resources for foraging and habitat dispersal (Goddard et al. 2010; Noordijk et al. 2010). A high amount of vegetated areas in urban areas, even small and isolated patches, can increase abundance and richness of arthropods (Turrini and Knop 2015). Vegetated solar parking canopies may serve such functions. Parking lots are often relatively large urban areas that break up and disconnect small and large vegetation patches. By providing built structures that provide shade and habitat area, especially when integrated with vegetation, solar canopies may act as steppingstones that help to alleviate habitat fragmentation. Other research has found that green roofs in urban areas can serve such a function by increasing habitat connectivity for arthropods (Braaker et al. 2014).

Urban green spaces – whether small and informal areas such as green roofs and those integrated with solar parking canopies, or parks and community gardens – are important in providing ecosystem services (Rupprecht et al. 2015). These green spaces and their integration with the built environment support ecosystem functioning and are part of urban ecological infrastructure that provides essential services such as air purification, moderation of climate extremes, biodiversity preservation, and human health benefits (Aronson et al. 2017; GomezBaggethun et al. 2013; Lepczyk et al. 2017; Maas et al. 2006). Our findings demonstrate that solar canopies – especially vegetated ones – are beneficial in this urban ecological infrastructure, providing habitat for and supporting arthropods that serve important functional roles in urban ecosystems.

While parking lots with solar canopies may not be as important for biodiversity conservation as other urban green spaces (e.g. larger and natural habitat fragments) (McIntyre 2000; Noordijk et al. 2010), this study indicates that the management of solar canopies may be important for enhancing arthropod abundance and connectivity between other vegetated areas. The presence of vegetated solar canopies likely offers more habitat than parking lots without such solar arrays

that offer little to no habitat for biodiversity (U.S. EPA 2008). We could not find any evidence in the literature or from the solar industry that arthropods under solar canopies damage them or affect their operation or energy output. Rather, some researchers and farmers are looking to integrate vegetation with rural, utility-scale solar energy facilities to serve as habitat for pollinators (Walston et al. 2018).

This study has several implications for urban ecosystem management, planning for ecosystem services, and biodiversity conservation. The expansion of urban renewable energy, and especially solar parking canopies, is an opportunity for a proactive reconciliation ecology approach. As urban area governments build solar energy in their own parking lots and as they consider permits for such development from businesses, schools, and other entities (Gagnon et al. 2016), they have an opportunity to transform large impervious surfaces from being ecologically detrimental to providing ecosystem benefits (U.S. EPA 2008). Whereas finding the impetus and resources to “green” parking lots and integrate vegetation may be unlikely from an ecological interest alone, factoring in such goals to renewable energy development that would occur regardless is a minimally burdensome addition. Our findings demonstrate that this design choice is worthwhile for the sake of arthropods that are beneficial for urban ecosystems, and that integrating flowering plants with solar canopies may be particularly worthwhile.[3]

Scholars have pointed to serious governance and management challenges facing cities in making progress on biodiversity conservation (Puppim de Oliveira et al. 2011). While renewable energy is just one of many considerations for urban areas and biodiversity planning, our findings indicate that solar parking canopies are an opportunity to link climate change policymaking, local economic development, and ecosystem conservation. Developed with an eye toward such matters, urban solar parking canopies can make solar energy advantageous not only in terms of GHG emission reductions but also for urban ecosystems, underscoring the importance of pursuing multiple sustainable development goals simultaneously.

With urban governments increasingly looking to expand renewable energy development, it is important for urban planners, ecologists, and researchers to proactively consider and plan what that means for urban ecosystems and biodiversity. This study demonstrates that renewable energy development can be beneficial. Yet urban renewable energy development could also pose a range of challenges for urban ecosystems, particularly if it encroaches on existing and often limited green spaces. Just as parking lots are an easy place to site groundmounted solar arrays, so are parks, fields, and other

The presence of vegetation, as well as the solar canopies themselves, may also help alleviate heat island effects associated with parking lots (Aniello et al. 1995; Onishi et al. 2010).

We are not saying any urban renewable energy development is necessarily bad, but rather that ecological effects should be considered and opportunities for co-benefits should be sought out. We hope this study helps to begin a dialogue and further research into ecosystem implications and opportunities of increasing urban renewable energy development. We call for further studies about the effects and conservation opportunities of urban renewable energy development and best management practices. Specifically related to solar parking canopies, future research should investigate how to best integrate vegetation, including what vegetation best supports arthropod diversity in these settings and is beneficial from both an ecological and management perspective. Beyond solar parking canopies, researchers should study ground-mounted solar arrays in other urban areas, including parks, fields, and brownfield sites. More broadly, researchers should take a holistic approach to studying how renewable energy (including wind and other technologies) can best be integrated in urban areas and conservation approaches to ensure the best possible ecological outcomes.
